title: Smallest degree of a Keller counterexample in dimension 3
W: In 2026 the Jacobian conjecture was refuted in three variables. The first explicit counterexample (Alpöge's map) has polynomial degree 7. Wang's theorem says degree 2 is impossible. What is the smallest degree a counterexample in three variables can have? In particular, is there one of degree 3, 4 or 5?
M: Let $d_3$ be the least $d$ such that some polynomial map $F:\mathbb C^3\to\mathbb C^3$ with $\max_i\deg F_i=d$ and $\det DF\in\mathbb C^\times$ is not an automorphism. Wang's theorem gives $d_3\ge3$, and Alpöge's map gives $d_3\le7$. Determine $d_3$. In particular, decide whether $d_3\le5$.
why: Once the conjecture is false in dimension 3, the main remaining question is how much room counterexamples need. Wang's quadratic theorem and the Bass–Connell–Wright cubic-homogeneous reduction both point to low degree as the decisive regime. Settling $d_3$ means either proving the conjecture for all cubic, quartic or quintic maps in three variables, which would be new even for cubics, or finding a much smaller counterexample. The answer tells us whether the phenomenon is rigid or flexible.
diagnosis: A fine-grained refinement (JC(3,d) for 3<=d<=6) of a now-false conjecture. Bounded-degree cases are decidable by elimination and may fall to computation. The natural big sibling, JC in dimension 2, is famous.
what_changed: Nothing. The alternatives (cubic-only case, smallest dimension with a cubic counterexample) are equally narrow. A 2026 low-dimensional survey (2607.22198) poses no minimal-degree question.

title: Periodic optimal colourings of Cayley graphs of Z^2
W: Join two points of the integer grid when their difference lies in a fixed finite set D. If this graph can be properly coloured with k colours, can it always be coloured with k colours in a repeating, wallpaper-like pattern? On a line the answer is yes. For some infinite graphs built from trees it is no. The plane is the first open case, and a yes would also give an algorithm for the chromatic number.
M: For finite symmetric $D\subset\mathbb Z^2\setminus\{0\}$ let $G_D=\mathrm{Cay}(\mathbb Z^2,D)$ with $\chi(G_D)=k<\infty$. Must $G_D$ have a proper $k$-colouring invariant under a finite-index subgroup of $\mathbb Z^2$? Equivalently, does the $k$-colouring subshift $X_{D,k}\subset\{1..k\}^{\mathbb Z^2}$ always contain a periodic point? (A yes makes $\{(D,k):\chi(G_D)\le k\}$ decidable via compactness plus enumeration of periodic colourings. A no gives the first weakly aperiodic colouring subshift on $\mathbb Z^2$.) Same question for $\mathbb Z^d$, $d\ge3$.
why: Proper colourings of $G_D$ form a 2D subshift of finite type of a special kind. Its constraints are only of the form 'different colours at difference d', and they are symmetric under permuting the colours. General 2D SFTs can be aperiodic (Berger). Recent work on periodic colourings of quasi-transitive graphs (arXiv:2411.01951) proves that 2-ended graphs have periodic chi-colourings. The same paper builds a tree-like quasi-transitive graph with no periodic chi-colouring and leaves 1-ended graphs open. Z^2 is the canonical 1-ended amenable case. The question mirrors the periodic tiling conjecture, which holds in Z^2 (Bhattacharya) and fails in high dimension (Greenfeld-Tao), so the same dimensional dichotomy may appear here.
diagnosis: B mostly because it was never literature-checked, and because the decidability question (a) was the headline when it is really a corollary. The structural periodicity question (b) is the real problem.
what_changed: The periodicity question is now the headline and decidability a corollary. Added Z^d. Placed it in the 2024 periodic-colouring programme (2-ended solved, tree-like counterexample). No source found that settles Z^2.

title: L⁴ Strichartz on the surface of a cube
W: On a square torus, the L⁴ Strichartz estimate for the Schrödinger equation loses only ε derivatives (Bourgain). On general flat surfaces with cone points only a 1/4-derivative loss is known. Decide whether the cube surface, with eight cone points of angle 3π/2 that diffract waves, behaves like the torus.
M: Let $S$ be the surface of the unit cube with its flat metric, and $\Delta$ the Friedrichs extension of the Laplacian from $C_c^\infty(S\setminus\{\text{vertices}\})$. Decide whether for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $C_\varepsilon$ with $\|e^{it\Delta}f\|_{L^4([0,1]\times S)}\le C_\varepsilon\|f\|_{H^\varepsilon(S)}$ for all $f$.
why: The cube surface is an arithmetic surface with cone points. Its 'nonsingular' eigenfunctions lift to trigonometric polynomials (Greif–Kaplan–Strichartz–Wiese), but the singular ones are not explicit, and diffraction at the vertices spoils the lattice-counting proof used on the torus. Blair–Ford–Marzuola obtain a $1/p$ loss on all compact flat cone surfaces and suggest the loss is an artefact of their method. The cube is the simplest test case where arithmetic structure and diffraction compete.
diagnosis: One test case (the cube). The natural general statement, epsilon-loss on every compact flat cone surface, is essentially what Blair-Ford-Marzuola suggest in their Remark 1.3. So the general version is not novel, and the cube version is narrow.
what_changed: Nothing. The general version is already suggested by BFM, and it would also force L^4 eigenfunction bounds of order lambda^eps on every polygon (by doubling). It is far out of reach and is not a new question.

title: Critical NLS blow-up threshold on the cube surface
W: In the plane, the focusing cubic Schrödinger equation needs at least the ground-state mass to blow up. On the surface of a cube, each corner is a cone with total angle 3π/2, which can hold a 'three-quarter' ground state. So the blow-up threshold should drop to three quarters of the planar one, and the claim is that it does exactly that.
M: Let $S$ be the surface of the unit cube with its flat metric, and let $\Delta$ be the Friedrichs extension of the Laplace–Beltrami operator on $C_c^\infty(S\setminus\{\text{vertices}\})$. Let $Q$ be the ground state of $\Delta Q-Q+Q^3=0$ on $\mathbb R^2$, and put $m_*=\tfrac34\|Q\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^2)}^2$. For $iu_t+\Delta u+|u|^2u=0$ on $S$, prove: (i) every $u_0\in H^1(S)$ with $\|u_0\|_2^2<m_*$ gives a global $H^1$ solution; (ii) for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $u_0\in H^1(S)$ with $m_*<\|u_0\|_2^2<m_*+\varepsilon$ whose solution blows up in finite time. (Stronger, optional: blow-up data exist for every mass $m>m_*$; also decide whether there is blow-up at mass exactly $m_*$.)
why: The sharp Gagliardo–Nirenberg constant on a cone of angle alpha <= 2*pi should be (alpha/2*pi) times the planar one, with the radial Q as extremiser. If so, conical singularities lower the mass threshold for collapse, and the cube surface turns this into a clean statement with an explicit constant. A proof would test the mass-critical blow-up theory (Weinstein, Merle–Raphaël, Burq–Gérard–Tzvetkov) on singular geometries, where existing Strichartz estimates come with loss.
diagnosis: Part (i) is routine given a sharp cone Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality and symmetrisation. Part (ii) adapts known near-threshold blow-up constructions (Burq-Gerard-Tzvetkov, Merle) to a vertex. The answer is predicted, and the cube is an arbitrary instance.
what_changed: Nothing. The general form, threshold (min(alpha_min,2pi)/2pi)||Q||^2 on any compact cone surface or Neumann polygon, is equally predictable. Searches found no prior statement, but it is a technical extension.

title: Does an oscillating source lower the Strauss exponent?
W: For the 3D wave equation with source |u|^p, small smooth data give global solutions exactly when p > 1+√2 (Strauss). Multiply the source by a factor that oscillates periodically in time with average zero, such as cos t. The global-existence proof still works above 1+√2. Every blow-up proof below it breaks, because they all need the source to be positive. Is the true threshold strictly smaller?
M: Let $g$ be smooth, $2\pi$-periodic, $\int_0^{2\pi}g=0$, $g\not\equiv0$ (model case $g=\cos t$). For $u_{tt}-\Delta u=g(t)|u|^p$ on $\mathbb R^{1+3}$ with data $\varepsilon(f,h)$, $f,h\in C_c^\infty$, let $p_c(g)=\inf\{p>1:\forall f,h,\ $the solution is global for all small $\varepsilon\}$. John-type estimates use only $|g|u|^p|\lesssim|u|^p$, so $p_c(g)\le1+\sqrt2$. Is $p_c(g)<1+\sqrt2$? Determine $p_c(g)$ (a resonance heuristic predicts $2$, independent of $g$). Also: for $1<p<p_c$, is the lifespan finite for suitable data?
why: The Strauss exponent is a central small-data threshold for nonlinear waves. Every proof of the blow-up half (John, Glassey, Sideris, Zhou, Yordanov-Zhang) uses the positivity of the source, while the global half uses only its size. A mean-zero oscillating factor separates the two. Either the threshold is robust, which would need a new blow-up mechanism, or the iteration along the light cone is suppressed by cancellation and the threshold is set by parametric resonance. In the second case u decays like 1/t near the cone, so |u|^{p-1} acts as a time-periodic potential of size t^{1-p}. Its Mathieu-type amplification is exp(c∫t^{1-p}dt), which diverges iff p<=2. The literature on g(t)|u|^p treats g>=0 or g of power type. Time-oscillating nonlinearities are studied for NLS (Cazenave-Scialom type averaging) but not, as far as I could find, at fixed frequency for the Strauss problem.
diagnosis: The original was one arbitrary coefficient (cos t) with an open-ended 'determine p_c'. Its novelty had not been checked against the literature.
what_changed: Generalised to any smooth periodic mean-zero g. Noted the free bound p_c<=1+√2 and made the headline the yes/no 'is p_c<1+√2?'. Searches on oscillating time-dependent coefficients in the Strauss problem found no prior treatment.

title: Deciding rationality of PL rotation numbers
W: A circle homeomorphism made of finitely many straight pieces, with rational break points and slopes, has a rotation number. Rational rotation numbers can be confirmed by finding a rational periodic orbit. Irrational ones occur too: Belk–Hyde–Moore found √2−1 with slopes 3/2, 2/3, 1. Is there an algorithm that always decides which case holds?
M: Let $\mathcal P$ be the set of orientation-preserving PL homeomorphisms of $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with finitely many rational break points, rational slopes and $f(0)\in\mathbb Q$, encoded by these data. Is $\{f\in\mathcal P:\rho(f)\in\mathbb Q\}$ decidable? (It is computably enumerable: if $\rho(f)=p/q$, the zero set of the lift $F^q(x)-x-p$ is a nonempty finite union of rational points and rational intervals.)
why: Rotation numbers of rational PL maps link Thompson-like groups $T_q$, renormalisation, and number theory. Belk–Hyde–Moore conjecture that the irrational values are quadratic when slopes are powers of one rational, and they ask about decidability for one-parameter families and for finite order in $T_q$. A decision procedure would amount to a structure theorem for when renormalisation of such maps fails to close up.
diagnosis: The decidability question sits right beside Belk-Hyde-Moore's own Questions 3-4 (deciding within the family f_{q,r}, finite order in T_q). The structural core, which irrationals occur as rotation numbers, is their Question 5 and Conjecture 1, so it is already posed.
what_changed: Nothing. Recasting it as the structural question would just restate BHM Question 5 and Conjecture 1. A 2025 PL-circle-map paper (2505.13689) does not touch decidability.

title: Sofa stability
W: Baek (2024) proved that Gerver's sofa has the largest area among shapes that can be moved around a right-angled corner in a hallway of width 1. Show that any movable sofa whose area is nearly Gerver's must be nearly Gerver's sofa in shape (which in particular gives uniqueness).
M: A moving sofa is a compact connected $S\subset\mathbb R^2$ that can be moved by a continuous rigid motion from $(-\infty,0]\times[0,1]$ to $[0,1]\times(-\infty,0]$ inside $L=((-\infty,1]\times[0,1])\cup([0,1]\times(-\infty,1])$. Let $G$ be Gerver's sofa, of area $A_G\approx2.21953$. Prove that there are $C,\alpha>0$ such that every moving sofa $S$ with $|S|\ge A_G-\varepsilon$ satisfies $\min_{g}|gS\,\triangle\,G|\le C\varepsilon^{\alpha}$, the minimum over rigid motions $g$ of the plane.
why: Baek's proof gives optimality, but its abstract claims neither uniqueness nor stability. A quantitative stability inequality is the standard sharpening of an isoperimetric-type theorem, as for Bonnesen-type and Fusco-Maggi-Pratelli results, and would make the solution robust, for example for numerical verification.
diagnosis: A stability or uniqueness add-on to Baek's optimality theorem. It is a technical follow-up that depends on verification of a 119-page proof. The natural sibling, the ambidextrous sofa (Romik), is a known open problem, not a novel one.
what_changed: Nothing. The stability formulation is already the right one (symmetric difference). Even qualitative uniqueness is still unclaimed in the abstract.

why: Advection and vortex stretching are the same size under scaling, and their competition decides regularity in 1D Euler models. In the De Gregorio, Cordoba-Cordoba-Fontelos and Okamoto-Sakajo-Wunsch models, the sign and relative weight of stretching flip the answer between blow-up and regularity (Elgindi-Jeong). This is the full 3D analogue: it isolates the sign of stretching while keeping the true nonlocal Biot-Savart structure.
diagnosis: An ad hoc model. Reversing the stretching destroys div omega = 0, so the system is not a geometric fluid model. Its natural swirl-free axisymmetric reduction (r*omega_theta transported) fits the studied family omega/r^{d-2}, where d=4 has recent results, and is a minor variant.
what_changed: Nothing. I found no 3D treatment of the reversed-stretching model, but every cleaner version is either a parameter variant of studied axisymmetric families or a 1D OSW model.

title: Non-arithmetic tones of the cube
W: Many vibration frequencies of a cube's surface come from flat tori and are rational multiples of pi squared. Prove that at least one frequency is not of this form.
M: Let $S$ be the boundary of the unit cube $[0,1]^3$ with its intrinsic flat metric (8 cone points of angle $3\pi/2$), and let $\Delta$ be the Friedrichs extension of the Laplacian on $S$. Prove that some eigenvalue of $\Delta$ is not in $\pi^2\mathbb{Q}$.
why: Flat cone surfaces whose cone angles are not of the form 2pi/k cannot be quotients of tori. Numerics show 'singular' eigenfunctions, non-smooth at the vertices, with eigenvalues that look non-arithmetic. Proving that even one of them is non-arithmetic would separate diffractive spectral geometry from lattice-arithmetic behaviour, in the simplest Platonic example.
diagnosis: Narrow and transcendence-flavoured, with little leverage: proving that one eigenvalue of one surface lies outside pi^2 Q has no clear consequence. The general version for non-torus-quotient cone surfaces is just as hard and no more natural.

title: KdV with a cosine coefficient
W: Put a cos x in front of the cubic term of the modified KdV equation on the circle. The energy and the mean are still conserved, but the L² norm is not, and the energy no longer has a definite sign. Can smooth solutions blow up in finite time?
M: Consider $u_t+u_{xxx}+(\cos(x)\,u^3)_x=0$ on $\mathbb T=\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z$ with real $u_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb T)$. It is Hamiltonian, $u_t=\partial_x\frac{\delta H}{\delta u}$ with $H=\int(\tfrac12u_x^2-\tfrac14\cos(x)u^4)$, and conserves $\int u$ and $H$. However, $\frac{d}{dt}\int u^2=\frac12\int\sin(x)u^4$. Decide whether every such $u_0$ yields a global smooth solution, or whether $\|u(t)\|_{H^1}\to\infty$ in finite time for some $u_0$.
why: Standard mKdV on the torus is globally well-posed because L² conservation and the L²-subcritical Gagliardo–Nirenberg inequality control the energy. A spatially varying coefficient breaks the translation symmetry and so the L² law, which removes the a priori bound. Any blow-up would have to come from L² growth rather than L² concentration. That is a mechanism of real interest for inhomogeneous dispersive equations, and this is about the simplest model where it could occur.
diagnosis: Cos x is an arbitrary coefficient. The underlying question, whether a variable-coefficient focusing nonlinearity can make L^2-subcritical mKdV on T blow up through L^2 growth, is a reasonable specialist question but not of broad interest.
what_changed: Nothing. If kept, state it for general smooth nonconstant a(x) that is positive somewhere: d/dt||u||^2=(1/2)∫a'u^4, and the bounds close only to dM/dt<~M^3. Literature search inconclusive.
